02 / Cyber Attacks on Healthcare

Cyber Attacks on Healthcare

Beyond physical attacks in conflict zones, healthcare systems face a growing wave of digital threats.

Ransomware

Hospitals Held Hostage

Encrypts patient records and locks clinical systems until paid — often forcing hospitals to divert ambulances and delay care.

DDoS

Overwhelming the Network

Floods hospital networks and patient portals with traffic, knocking scheduling and telehealth systems offline when care teams need them most.

Infrastructure Hijack

Connected, Exposed Systems

Targets connected medical devices and building-control systems — from HVAC and power to networked diagnostic equipment.

Data Breach

Records at Risk

Exposes patient histories, insurance details, and personal identifiers — among the most valuable, long-lasting data on the black market.

05 / About Us

Why This Matters

Background on the legal, humanitarian, and structural context behind the index.

Background

Background: Why This Matters

Under international humanitarian law, including the Geneva Conventions, healthcare systems are supposed to be granted protection during armed conflict. Hospitals, medical personnel, and medical units must not be targeted under any circumstances.

Despite these legal protections, attacks on healthcare continue to occur as tensions rise globally and new conflicts erupt. The Medical Security Index was created to better understand these risks by analyzing conflict intensity, healthcare system capacity, displacement pressures, and demographic vulnerability.

What We Do

What the Medical Security Index Does

By combining conflict data, healthcare system capacity indicators, and displacement pressures, the index identifies environments where medical systems may face elevated structural stress — giving researchers and policymakers insight into how conflict and cyber threats affect global healthcare infrastructure.

Digital Threats

Cyber Attacks on Healthcare

Healthcare systems store sensitive patient information and rely heavily on digital infrastructure, making them attractive targets for cyber criminals. Attacks can disrupt hospital operations, compromise patient safety, and expose confidential medical records — challenges compounded by limited resources and outdated systems.

06 / FAQs

Frequently Asked Questions

Find answers to commonly asked questions about our research.

Q.What is the Medical Security Index?

An independent research initiative that tracks and analyzes threats to healthcare systems worldwide, using verified data to understand how conflict and cyber threats disrupt healthcare delivery.

Q.How do attacks disrupt healthcare?

Attacks can damage facilities, interrupt surgeries and routine treatments, displace healthcare workers, disrupt supply chains, and damage infrastructure such as electricity and water systems.

Q.Where does your data come from?

Verified and publicly available sources, including international organizations, healthcare reporting networks, and documented case studies, cross-referenced and standardized before inclusion.

Q.How can this research help?

By highlighting structural risks in conflict and crisis environments, the index provides insights that support research, policy discussions, and efforts to strengthen healthcare protections.

Q.Is this data publicly available?

Yes. Our interactive map and research findings are publicly accessible to researchers, policymakers, healthcare professionals, and the broader public.

Q.What makes the Index different?

It combines conflict intensity, healthcare system capacity, internal displacement, and demographic vulnerability — few existing datasets integrate all of these factors together.

04 / Methodology

Data & Methodology

The full Healthcare System Stress Flag (HSSF) Version 1.0 framework — how it's built, what it measures, and where it falls short.

Healthcare System Stress Flag — Version 1.0

The Healthcare System Stress Flag, or HSSF, is the Medical Security Index’s primary analytical framework for identifying countries where multiple structural pressures may place healthcare systems under elevated stress.

While many existing global indices measure conflict or healthcare capacity independently, the HSSF was designed to capture the interaction between conflict exposure and healthcare system resilience.

The framework combines country-level data on armed conflict, internal displacement, healthcare capacity, access to essential services, and population structure.

HSSF is designed as a comparative screening tool. It is not a clinical measure, predictive model, measure of healthcare quality, or forecast of health-system collapse.

Healthcare systems may face increasing structural pressure when several forms of vulnerability occur at the same time. HSSF Version 1.0 examines six dimensions:

Conflict intensity Conflict persistence Internal displacement Hospital-bed capacity Skilled birth attendance Population age structure

The framework does not assume that any one indicator can explain healthcare-system stress on its own. Instead, it identifies countries where several measurable stressors coexist.

A High or Extreme classification does not mean that a healthcare system has collapsed. A Low classification does not mean that a country is free from healthcare, humanitarian, or security challenges.

HSSF is intended to support:

  • Comparative research
  • Public-health and humanitarian analysis
  • Policy discussion
  • Journalism and public communication
  • The identification of countries that may warrant closer study

The Version 1.0 MSI dataset includes 50 countries selected through purposive sampling based on:

  • Relevance to conflict-related healthcare-system stress
  • The presence of conflict, displacement, healthcare-capacity, or demographic pressures
  • The availability of core indicators

The sample is intended for exploratory comparative analysis. It is not representative of every country globally and should not be interpreted as a complete global ranking. Future versions may adopt a more systematic country-inclusion rule as MSI expands its coverage and strengthens its data-completeness requirements.

The HSSF calculation follows four steps.

1. Normalize

Indicators that depend on national population size are converted into per-capita rates or percentages. This allows countries of different population sizes to be compared more consistently.

2. Evaluate

Each indicator is assessed against a fixed Version 1.0 operational threshold.

3. Score

A country receives one point for every threshold it meets. All six indicators are equally weighted.

4. Classify

The points are added to produce a total score from 0 to 6. That score is then converted into one of four HSSF classifications:

Low Moderate High Extreme
Analytical Dimension

Conflict intensity

Definition

Conflict deaths per 100,000 measures the number of fatalities associated with state-based armed conflict relative to a country’s population. Population adjustment makes it possible to compare conflict intensity across countries with substantially different population sizes.

Why it is included

High levels of conflict mortality may indicate an environment in which healthcare systems face greater disruption. Conflict can affect:

Hospitals and clinics Emergency medical services Healthcare staffing Transportation and referral systems Medical supply chains Electricity and water infrastructure Access to routine and preventive care

This indicator does not directly count attacks on healthcare facilities or personnel. It measures the broader intensity of the state-based conflict environment.

Primary Data Sources

State-based conflict fatalities: Uppsala Conflict Data Program
Population denominator: World Health Organization country data

Reference Period

State-based conflict fatalities: 2024
Population denominator: 2023

Calculation

Conflict deaths per 100,000 = State-based conflict fatalities / Population × 100,000

Version 1.0 Threshold

5 or more conflict deaths per 100,000 people

Scoring Rule

Threshold met: 1 point
Threshold not met: 0 points

Threshold Rationale

The threshold is intended to identify countries experiencing comparatively elevated population-adjusted conflict intensity. It is an operational Version 1.0 decision and has not yet been statistically optimized or externally calibrated.

Limitations

UCDP state-based conflict data does not represent every form of violence or insecurity. It may not fully capture:

  • Non-state violence
  • Communal violence
  • Criminal violence
  • Low-intensity instability
  • Localized violence below the dataset’s reporting thresholds

A national rate may also obscure severe conflict concentrated within particular regions.

Analytical Dimension

Conflict persistence

Definition

Years of sustained conflict measures the number of years between 2015 and 2024 in which a country met MSI’s active-conflict criterion. A qualifying year is one in which the country recorded at least 25 state-based conflict fatalities. Qualifying years do not need to be consecutive.

Why it is included

Conflict can weaken healthcare systems gradually as well as through sudden shocks. Persistent conflict may contribute to:

accumulated infrastructure damage healthcare-worker displacement interrupted medical education weakened public institutions reduced investment prolonged supply shortages and recurring interruptions to routine care

This indicator captures duration across time rather than the intensity of one year.

Primary Data Sources

Uppsala Conflict Data Program

Reference Period

2015–2024

Calculation

For each year in the ten-year period:

  • At least 25 state-based conflict fatalities: qualifying year
  • Fewer than 25 fatalities: non-qualifying year

The qualifying years are then added together.

Version 1.0 Threshold

7 or more qualifying years between 2015 and 2024

Scoring Rule

Threshold met: 1 point
Threshold not met: 0 points

Threshold Rationale

Seven qualifying years indicates sustained exposure across most of the ten-year reference period. The threshold is intended to distinguish persistent conflict environments from countries experiencing shorter or more isolated periods of state-based conflict.

Limitations

The indicator does not distinguish between:

  • continuous conflict and intermittent conflict
  • geographically widespread conflict and localized conflict
  • or lower-intensity persistence and shorter periods of extreme violence
Analytical Dimension

Displacement pressure

Definition

Conflict-related IDPs per 100,000 measures the stock of people internally displaced by conflict and violence relative to the national population. Internally displaced people remain within their country’s borders but may lose access to housing, employment, medication, sanitation, transportation, and established healthcare networks.

Why it is included

Large-scale displacement can simultaneously increase demand for healthcare and weaken continuity of access. Displacement may:

  • concentrate demand in receiving communities
  • interrupt treatment for chronic conditions
  • increase maternal and child-health needs
  • weaken vaccination continuity
  • increase exposure to communicable disease
  • and place additional pressure on hospitals and clinics
Primary Data Sources

Conflict-related displacement stock: Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC)
Population denominator: World Health Organization country data

Reference Period

Conflict-related displacement stock: 2024
Population denominator: 2023

Calculation

IDPs per 100,000 = Conflict-related IDPs / Population × 100,000

Version 1.0 Threshold

5,000 or more IDPs per 100,000 people. This is equivalent to approximately 5% of the national population.

Scoring Rule

Threshold met: 1 point
Threshold not met: 0 points

Threshold Rationale

The threshold is intended to identify countries where internal displacement represents a substantial share of the national population and may place meaningful pressure on healthcare access and service demand.

Limitations

IDP stock is a point-in-time measure. It does not fully capture:

new displacement flows repeated displacement displacement duration returns living conditions geographic concentration or actual access to healthcare

National rates may conceal much more severe regional pressures.

Analytical Dimension

Healthcare capacity

Definition

Hospital beds per 1,000 people measures reported inpatient-bed capacity relative to population size.

Why it is included

Hospital-bed density provides a broad indication of the physical capacity available for inpatient treatment. Limited capacity may become more consequential when healthcare systems face:

  • trauma cases
  • outbreaks
  • damaged facilities
  • displacement
  • interruptions to primary care
  • or shortages of functioning medical infrastructure
Primary Data Sources

World Bank World Development Indicators

Reference Period

Latest available country-year used in the Version 1.0 database. The exact reference year may differ by country.

Version 1.0 Threshold

Fewer than 1 hospital bed per 1,000 people

Scoring Rule

Threshold met: 1 point
Threshold not met: 0 points

Threshold Rationale

The threshold identifies countries with especially limited reported inpatient capacity. It is an operational Version 1.0 benchmark and should not be interpreted as a universal standard for healthcare-system adequacy.

Limitations

Hospital-bed density does not measure:

whether beds are operational healthcare-worker availability equipment or medication geographic accessibility quality of care occupancy rates affordability or specialist capacity

A country may have relatively high reported bed density and still experience serious healthcare-system stress.

Analytical Dimension

Access to essential healthcare services

Definition

Skilled birth attendance measures the percentage of births attended by personnel trained to provide essential childbirth care.

Why it is included

The indicator provides a broad proxy for access to essential health services and functioning maternal-health infrastructure. Lower coverage may reflect challenges involving:

healthcare access workforce availability geographic inequality facility coverage transportation affordability continuity of care

Maternal-health services may be particularly vulnerable to conflict, displacement, and infrastructure disruption.

Primary Data Sources

World Bank World Development Indicators

Reference Period

Latest available country-year used in the Version 1.0 dataset. The exact reference year may vary by country.

Version 1.0 Threshold

Below 70%

Scoring Rule

Threshold met: 1 point
Threshold not met: 0 points

Threshold Rationale

The threshold is intended to identify countries where a substantial share of births may occur without skilled attendance. It is an operational Version 1.0 rule and is not presented as a universal international cut-point.

Limitations

Skilled birth attendance represents one dimension of healthcare access. It does not fully measure:

  • quality of childbirth care
  • emergency obstetric capacity
  • rural–urban disparities
  • informal care
  • current disruption occurring after the source year
Analytical Dimension

Demographic vulnerability

Definition

This indicator measures the percentage of a country’s population below age 15.

Why it is included

A younger population structure may create greater demand for:

pediatric care vaccination maternal and reproductive health services nutrition programs infectious-disease prevention primary care

When combined with conflict, displacement, or limited capacity, this demand may contribute to structural pressure on healthcare systems.

Primary Data Sources

World Bank World Development Indicators

Reference Period

Latest available country-year used in the Version 1.0 dataset. The exact reference year may vary by country.

Version 1.0 Threshold

40% or more of the population under age 15

Scoring Rule

Threshold met: 1 point
Threshold not met: 0 points

Threshold Rationale

The threshold identifies countries with particularly young population structures and potentially elevated demand for maternal, pediatric, preventive, and primary healthcare services.

Limitations

A young population does not itself indicate healthcare-system weakness. Its relevance within HSSF comes from its interaction with the other structural pressures measured by the framework.

Indicator-specific normalization

HSSF does not use statistical standardization.

  • Instead, MSI uses indicator-specific conversions when necessary
  • Conflict fatalities are expressed per 100,000 people
  • Conflict-related displacement is expressed per 100,000 people
  • Population under age 15 is expressed as a percentage
  • Skilled birth attendance is expressed as a percentage
  • Hospital-bed density is already expressed as a population-adjusted rate

After these conversions, indicators are evaluated against fixed thresholds. The term normalization refers to per-capita or percentage conversion, not statistical normalization.

No imputation

MSI does not:

  • Replace missing values with zero
  • Statistically estimate missing observations
  • Assume that unavailable data indicate the absence of stress

Only genuine zero values reported by the source dataset are recorded as zero.

Equal weighting and calculation:

Each indicator contributes one point. No indicator receives additional weight.

Indicator scoring function
Ii = { 1,if the Version 1.0 threshold is met 0,if the threshold is not met

The total HSSF score is:

Total HSSF score
HSSF score = 6 Σ i=1 Ii

The minimum possible score is 0. The maximum possible score is 6.

Equal weighting was selected to:

Improve transparency Support reproducibility Avoid unsupported weighting decisions Keep Version 1.0 easy to interpret

Equal weighting does not imply that the six indicators have equal real-world or causal importance.

HSSF classifications:

Underlying HSSF scoreClassification
0–1Low
2–3Moderate
4–5High
6Extreme

The classification scale is ordinal: Low → Moderate → High → Extreme

Display Coding

Some figures and maps may encode the four classifications numerically:

Display codeClassification
1Low
2Moderate
3High
4Extreme

The 1–4 display code is used only for visualization. It is not the underlying HSSF score, which ranges from 0 to 6.

Version 1.0

HSSF Version 1.0 was developed before MSI adopted a formal complete-data eligibility policy. Some Version 1.0 classifications were retained despite missing values in the primary dataset. These classifications should be interpreted as provisional and will be reassessed in a future methodological release.

Future releases

Beginning with the next HSSF version: A country must have values for all six component indicators to receive a classification.

Countries with one or more unresolved missing indicators will be labeled: Insufficient Data

Insufficient Data does not indicate low healthcare-system stress or low humanitarian need. It means that MSI cannot calculate the HSSF consistently using all six required indicators.

When a primary standardized dataset does not provide a required observation, MSI may consider an approved alternate source.

Potential alternate sources include:

  1. Official national health ministries
  2. National statistical authorities
  3. United Nations agencies
  4. Other intergovernmental organizations
  5. Peer-reviewed research
  6. Recognized humanitarian or healthcare research organizations

An alternate value may only be used when:

  • it measures the same indicator
  • its unit is compatible with the HSSF definition
  • the reference year is documented
  • the geographic coverage is appropriate
  • the methodology or source record is publicly accessible
  • and the substitution undergoes internal review before publication
Data statusMeaning
StandardisedAll six indicators use MSI’s primary datasets
SupplementedAt least one indicator uses an approved alternate source
Insufficient DataOne or more required indicators remain unavailable

Countries using alternate-source data should be identified in MSI’s technical records.

Alternate values may differ from primary standardized datasets in:

collection methods reporting periods geographic coverage definitions

HSSF is intended to help answer: Where do multiple measurable structural pressures coexist?

It is not intended to answer:

  • Which country has the best or worst healthcare system?
  • Whether a healthcare system will collapse
  • Whether a country is safe
  • Whether one indicator causes another
  • Whether a government is responsible for observed conditions
  • How healthcare stress is distributed within every region of a country

HSSF classifications should be interpreted alongside:

The underlying indicator values Country context Data availability Humanitarian reporting Framework’s stated limitations

HSSF Version 1.0 has several important limitations.

Operational thresholds

The six thresholds are research-team-defined and have not yet been statistically validated or externally calibrated.

Equal weighting

All indicators contribute one point, although their real-world effects may differ across countries and settings.

Mixed reference years

Some health indicators use the latest available observation, meaning values may refer to different years across countries.

National-level analysis

National averages may conceal major differences between regions, cities, displacement sites, and conflict-affected communities.

Conflict-data coverage

UCDP state-based conflict data does not capture every form of violence, insecurity, or humanitarian disruption.

Displacement measurement

IDP stock does not fully represent displacement flows, repeated displacement, duration, returns, or living conditions.

Healthcare capacity

Hospital-bed density does not measure functionality, staffing, supplies, quality, occupancy, or geographic access.

Essential-service access

Skilled birth attendance represents one part of healthcare access and does not measure the entire health system.

Demographic interpretation

A young population is not itself evidence of healthcare-system weakness.

Attacks on healthcare

HSSF Version 1.0 does not directly include a coded indicator for attacks on healthcare facilities, personnel, or transports.

Cybersecurity

Healthcare cybersecurity is an expanding MSI research area but is not included in the HSSF Version 1.0 calculation.

Missing data

Data gaps may limit classification, particularly in countries experiencing severe conflict or institutional disruption.
